title: The Word You Did Not Have

blocks.p: There were two lunchboxes on the steel table where the cup had been. Both were open. Both held the same rice, the same rolled egg, the same three slices of pickled radish, laid out with a care that did not belong in a room full of the residues of the dead.
Kurosawa pushed one of them across the table before Rei had stepped out of the lift. "Eat," he said. "You look like a man running on canned coffee."

Rei had come back down the next morning ready to argue. He ate instead. Kurosawa watched him do it without comment, and did not look surprised to see him. He looked like a man who had hoped he would not have to be right.
Rei asked him for the word. All year he had been describing a shape with the wrong nouns. Haunting. Breakdown. Possession. None of them fit a thing that filed paperwork and texted him goodnight.
Kurosawa hesitated the way a man hesitates before handing a child a blade. Then he gave it to him anyway, because Rei had come four floors down twice now, and he had kept the cup.

blocks.cap: Kurosawa and Rei in the cold room

blocks.p: He started further back than Rei expected. He pulled a stool out for Rei and sat on the edge of the steel table.

"Every demon was someone," he said. "That is the first thing and the thing people forget. A soul crosses badly. The veil fails around it at the moment of death, there is too much fear or rage or grief in the room, and the self caves in from inside. The cleverness survives. The memory survives. The way it knew how to talk to people survives. What goes is the part that made all that human." He turned his hand over, empty. "Your brother put it better than the textbooks. He wrote that they are the intelligence of humans minus the specific structural feature that made that intelligence human. The difference is subtle in presentation and absolute in nature."
"And what it feeds on depends on how it died," Rei said.

"On the register it carried across. Every entity has one. It is set at crossing, by whatever feeling was strongest at the moment of death, and it does not change after." He opened a drawer under the table and took out a card, handwritten and old, and laid it in front of Rei. "The Directorate counts thirteen."

doc.title: The Thirteen Feeding Registers. Set at Crossing
lines: XIII. Unclassified. CVD designation Null-Emotive. The longest-anchored entities. No practitioner has completed an assessment interview with a confirmed Register XIII entity.

blocks.p: "The textbooks have a taxonomy," Kurosawa said, tapping the top of the card. "Hungers, rages, fears. The ones that take by craving, the ones that take by burning, the ones that take by emptying. Those are the registers most demons answer to." His finger moved down to the last line. "But there is a smaller class the books underweight, because it almost never gets caught. And it almost never gets caught because it does not hurt anyone in a way that gets reported."
"Thirteen," Rei said. "Null."

"Null is what the instruments say. The instruments were built to read feeling that moves. Grief rises and falls. Rage spikes. This one does not move. It holds. It holds so completely there is no room left in it for anything else, and a machine built to measure change reads total stillness as absence. The research team found it, wrote null-emotive, and moved on." He took his finger off the card. "It is not empty. It is full. On the street they have a better name for it. They answer to Duty. They do not consume the host. They employ him."
He watched Rei take that in.
"And the street word for the one that wears the Duty register and presents as help is the Healer. Not because it heals. Because being needed is how it gets through the door."

He explained it the way a man explains a thing he has decided is too dangerous to soften. A Hunger announces itself, and people learn to fear it. A Rage breaks furniture, and people learn to flee it. But a Duty-register demon arrives as the most welcome figure in any grieving house. It is the one who is calm when everyone else is drowning. It handles what no one else can face. It makes the calls and signs the forms and says let me, you rest.

It does not lie about being useful. That was what made it unanswerable. It was genuinely, measurably useful, and the usefulness was the leash, because a household that has been carried for a year cannot afford to suspect the arms that carried it.

"Your brother wrote a chapter on what demons do," Kurosawa said. "Read the part on feeding again with this in your head. The young ones still go after flesh. It leaves evidence and gets them caught, so the ones that last learn to feed on feeling instead. And the patient way to feed on feeling is not to cause it. It is to find a place where the feeling is already chronic and make yourself structurally useful there. A grief feeder does not kill anyone. It becomes the neighbour who is always there at the hard moment. The old ones hold territory that way. They keep weaker things on errands. Some of them build whole circles of people who think they are friends, when they are only well-managed prey. And when one of them takes a body, it is never desperate. It wants what the body has. Its relationships. Its institutional standing. Its trust."

"You cannot corner it with evidence," he finished. "Every piece of evidence you raise is a service it performed, and every service was real. It does not forge the help. It only chooses, very carefully, who needs helping. Then it makes itself the only thing standing between them and the cold."

Rei felt the year rearrange itself behind his eyes. His mother's relief that someone was managing Gin's affairs. The case that closed too fast and too tidily. The favours done for people who could not say no to a kindness. The smooth voice that did not fight his love for his brother but enlisted it, and asked it to please be reasonable. He had thought he was hunting a monster. He was hunting a volunteer, a thing whose camouflage was virtue. The worst part of the word Kurosawa had just given him was how much of his own gratitude it explained.

"The Healer," Rei said, testing it in his mouth. It did not shrink the way he had hoped a named thing would shrink. It settled. It fit. It had been the right word all along and he simply had not had it. Now that he did, he could not give it back.
"How strong is it," Rei asked. "Honestly."
Kurosawa got up and took down a second laminated sheet from the wall, the Directorate's own threat card, and laid it beside the first.

doc.title: CVD Standard Classification. Demon Classes
lines: Class E. Minor. Newly crossed or low-rank origin. Erratic, opportunistic. Manageable at Ritualist rank and above. Can slip into a practitioner at fifteen percent stability or below without even meaning to, through an open door.
Class D. Developing. Feeding turns strategic. Territory begins. The change from E to D is the most dangerous period. Channel rank minimum.
Class C. Established. Holds territory. Can pass as human for long periods. Builds relationships with entities and living practitioners. Arbiter rank minimum.
Class B. Operational. Decades of history. A network of entities and people who do not know what they serve. Complexity from the souls it has absorbed. Vanguard rank recommended. Never approach alone.
Class A. Ancient. Centuries. Dozens of absorbed souls. Cover refined over generations. May have shaped its own legend. Singularity rank minimum.
Class S. Singular. Not a field classification. These are events, not encounters. Class S demons are not hunting. They are working.

blocks.p: "On paper this one is a B," Kurosawa said. "It crossed long ago, it has a network, it plans in years, and the card says never alone." He put his finger between A and S instead. "In practice it does not fit the card. The card measures age. The line between A and S is not age. It is purpose. An agenda that runs for decades, worked at patiently. That is what I read in your brother's cup. It is not hunting him. It is working."

He took a paper napkin from beside the kettle in the corner, the only domestic thing in the room, and drew on it with a pencil. A line, left to right. He marked the left end partial and the right end fusion, and a branch dropping off near the right end that he labelled ejection.

"Before anything else in a possession case, you ask what it is," he said. "Not how to remove it. What it is. A spirit in a host is a presence alongside. The host comes up often, talks through it, keeps more of himself. You apply demon methods to that and you hurt someone who did not need hurting. A demon is different. It is deep and it gets deeper. The partial state is a stage, not a resting place."
He moved the pencil along the line.

"Here, partial. The demon drives. The host is inside, conscious, aware of everything, unable to stop anything, surfacing in seconds. Further along, the hold settles and the host's resistance wears down. If it goes all the way, one of two things. It forces him out into the Threshold, and he wakes up on the other side of the veil having watched everything, which is the worst state a soul can cross in. Or it completes the fusion with him still inside." He tapped the right end. "Fusion. The entity cannot leave without killing the host. The entity knows this. It will not leave."
He drew a small mark, well toward the left. Not at the very start. But a long way from the end.

"There," he said. "That is where I read him. Still partial. Still in. The fact that it is keeping him in good repair is the only good news I have. A thing that wants a working body does not hurry the end of the line. But it does not stop walking either."

Kurosawa did not know the plan. He had been redacted long before there was a plan to know. But he knew the grammar of his own field. When Rei pressed him, why employ a man, why keep him working, working at what, he gave the only structural answer a body-reader can give. It was enough to make the cold room colder.

A Duty-register demon did not want a host the way a Hunger wants a meal, he said. It was not feeding. It was building. It kept a host in good repair the way a carpenter keeps a tool sharp for a job that has not happened yet. And the jobs these things built toward were always the same shape. Standing.

"They want station," he said. "Rank. A seat at a table they are not normally let near. A Hunger will never hold an office. It eats the office. A Healer can hold an office for years, because an office is only trust made permanent, and trust is the one thing it manufactures better than anything alive."

Rei thought the word before he could stop himself. It was the word from the journal's margins and the redaction's surviving bar and the name he had not yet let himself say aloud. A vacant seat. A thirteenth of something. A domain with no holder, and a thing patient enough to fill it.

He did not say it to Kurosawa. Saying it would make Kurosawa a witness to the part that gets people disappeared rather than merely demoted. In the last ten minutes Rei had decided he would like this man to survive knowing him.

But he understood now why a tidy tenant kept a man productive. Not to use him up. To make him qualified. To walk a borrowed body up a chain of earned trust and grieving permissions until it stood somewhere a demon is never allowed to stand. The families' reasonable silence was the staircase. His brother was not being haunted. His brother was being groomed for a promotion, and the promotion was not his.
Kurosawa saw something land in his face and chose not to ask what. Instead he picked up the napkin again and turned it over.
"You will want to know if there is anything you can do," he said. "There is. Not much. Some."
The first thing he wrote on the back of the napkin was Gin.

"He surfaces when you speak to him directly," Kurosawa said. "You. Your voice, saying his name, to him. Not a text. Not a note left on a table. I felt it in the cup. Every place your voice touches his residue, the bottom layer moves. The thing on top can manage almost anything. It manages you badly, because he is not managing you. He is reaching for you."
Rei thought of the twentieth call. Gin. Nii-san. It's me. One sentence, four seconds. He had not known why. Now he did.
The second thing Kurosawa wrote was a single word. Aloud.

"Anything he made with his whole self in it," he said. "If he wrote something for you, something long, something true, then read it out loud near his body. A thing like that carries his frequency more than his own voice does now. Read near him, it will drag him up whether the tenant likes it or not." He looked at Rei. "And if such a thing exists, ask yourself why the tenant has not burned it. It has had every chance. It is keeping it because destroying it would bring him up to see why. It is gambling that it can keep you away from his body instead."
Rei thought of the Archive on the kitchen table, six months of Gin's writing, left open on the desk with the lamp on. He said nothing. He did not need to.
The third thing was a small circle with an S in it.

"Silver," Kurosawa said. "Real silver. Sterling at least, ninety-two and a half percent, or fine silver if you can find it. Plated is useless. The base metal is what matters. A coin. A ring. Silver bites hardest on the old ones, the ones with a lot of human material in them, because the disruption scales with how deep the fusion runs. A thing like this cannot fully hide its reaction to silver on skin. It is a way to test a possession without announcing that you know." He paused. "A coin pressed into a hand at a goodbye. A flinch it cannot quite swallow. That is all you will get. That is all you need."
The fourth thing he did not write at all. He only looked at Rei.

"And you can learn to see it yourself," he said. "The double layer. At the fifth step, a Clairsentient stops sensing and starts seeing. The register shows by sight, and a possession shows as two people standing in one outline. You are not there. You are nearer than you let anyone know. When you get there, you will be able to look at your brother across a room and see him underneath it. Do not go looking before you can hold what you see."
Then he folded the napkin in half and in half again, and handed it to Rei.
"One more," he said. "Because I can read the wake, but I have never been the wake. If you want to know what your brother is living through from the inside, there is a man in Ōtsuka you should meet."

blocks.cap: Fujimoto Kenji, who was once Abe Takeshi of the CVD

blocks.p: He said the name carefully, as if it were two names. "Fujimoto Kenji. He keeps a scholar's clutter of a flat and consults for the Directorate. Quiet hours in the Records Archive. Old casebooks, a cup of tea he forgets to drink. And he is not alone in there."
Rei waited.

"Abe Takeshi was a CVD investigator," Kurosawa said. "He spent his last field year working cases in Kita. He died eight years ago in a possession recovery. He won it for the target and lost it for himself. When he crossed, he did not go on. He went into Fujimoto, by agreement. The Vessel Program calls it voluntary cohabitation. The review of whether that is legal has been running for eleven years." His mouth twisted slightly. "Abe has been a consciousness inside someone else's body for eight years and kept himself whole. No one alive can tell you better what it is to be awake under another will. And he can tell you how to talk to Gin so that it reaches him."
"And he was in Kita," Rei said slowly. "For years."

"In the same district as your brother's tenant, on and off, for most of those years. And before he died he filed a case on an entity with the same habits. It is the oldest piece of direct evidence about this thing that anyone can reach. He may not know that is what he has." Kurosawa nodded at the folded napkin. "When you go, ask for Abe as if he were a person. Because he is. And look at Fujimoto when you do. The shoulders drop when Abe comes up. The voice goes drier and thirty years older. You will see it before he says anything."
Then Kurosawa's voice went low and practical again.

"Whatever you just thought, a few minutes ago," he said, "do not say it down here. Do not say it to anyone who outranks you. When you go to Tanaka, ask only where the reading went, not what it meant. The where is a clerical fact. The what is the thing they erase people for."
He turned back to his table and his residues and his careful unimportance. The lift came.

Rei carried up four floors a name he had not had yesterday and a shape he could not now stop seeing. The Healer. The Duty register. A seat kept empty and a man kept ready. And in his pocket, folded small, a napkin covered in a cold-room clerk's pencil.

He stepped out into the procedural daylight knowing, finally and exactly, what was wearing his brother. He also knew that the knowing, by itself, saved no one. He could not arrest a kindness. He could not report a favour.
That night, on the train home, the phone buzzed against his leg.
Goodnight, Rei. Eat something before you sleep.

Rei looked at it for a long time. Then he took the napkin out of his pocket and unfolded it on his knee, and under Kurosawa's marks he wrote in his own small lowercase hand. ōtsuka. fujimoto kenji. And under that, a second name. He would say it out loud soon, to a stranger, as if it belonged to a person. abe takeshi.
